records.place: Oberhausen an der Nahe; the Hermannshöhle at Niederhausen, Nahe

wine.name: Niederhäuser Hermannshöhle Riesling GG
wine.classification: VDP.Grosses Gewächs from the Hermannshöhle, a VDP.Grosse Lage of Niederhausen
wine.sites: The Hermannshöhle at Niederhausen, a steep slope facing south to south west in a bend of the Nahe at about 130 to 175 metres, on black grey slate mixed with volcanic rock, porphyry and limestone.
wine.making: Picked by hand in selective passes. As the house's own sheets describe it, the wine is fermented and matured partly in stainless steel and partly in classic oak casks, and under the VDP's rule it is not released before September of the year after the harvest.
wine.glass: White peach, yellow apple and lime peel over wet stone and a smoky, flinty note from the slate and volcanic rock; dry, taut and long, with ripe acidity and a fine, salty finish.
wine.ageing: Open and bright on release, it often closes for a few years, then gains honey, quince and smoke, and a strong vintage keeps for twenty years and more.
wine.serve: 10 to 13 degrees Celsius; no need to decant, though a young bottle opens with air in the glass; a white wine glass.

label.means: The single vineyard at Niederhausen; the house's recent sheets print the site alone, older labels Niederhäuser Hermannshöhle.
Often shortened to GG: a dry wine of the VDP from a vineyard it ranks Grosse Lage.
Dry: the VDP requires every Grosses Gewächs to be dry by the legal measure.

records.table: Dönnhoff's Niederhäuser Hermannshöhle Riesling GG is the dry wine of the slope by which the Nahe has measured its other vineyards for a century: black grey slate and volcanic rock above the river. It is taut, smoky and long, so pour it cool rather than cold.
records.story: The Dönnhoff family came to Oberhausen on the Nahe around 1750, by the usual account, as farmers who kept livestock and gardens beside a few vines; the wine guide wein.plus dates the family's records as growers back to 1761. Over the generations the vines took over the farm. In 1971 a son of the house took the small estate on from his father, whose name it carries in its formal title, Weingut Hermann Dönnhoff, and over the following decades he grew it slowly, parcel by parcel. The parcel that mattered most lay in the neighbouring village, in the Hermannshöhle at Niederhausen, the site that the VDP says has been the Nahe's reference for more than a century, the measure by which its other vineyards are classified; the house tells how it bought prized plots there from a former head of the VDP on the Nahe. Beside it the house holds the Oberhäuser Brücke at Oberhausen as a monopole, the source of its sweet Spätlese and Eiswein. With the 2007 vintage the next generation took over the cellar. For a sommelier the Hermannshöhle Grosses Gewächs is the middle Nahe in one glass: slate and volcanic stone, dry, and made to keep.

others.name: Oberhäuser Brücke Riesling Spätlese
others.note: From the house's monopole at Oberhausen, the source of its sweet Spätlese, Auslese and Eiswein.

others.name: Felsenberg Felsentürmchen Riesling GG
others.note: From the Felsentürmchen parcel of the Felsenberg at Schlossböckelheim, on volcanic rock: the firmest of the house's dry wines.

others.name: Norheimer Dellchen Riesling GG
others.note: Steep volcanic and slate terraces at Norheim, a broader dry wine.

traps: The Hermannshöhle is Dönnhoff's site at Niederhausen; the Hermannsberg, also at Niederhausen, is the sole vineyard of Gut Hermannsberg.
The house sits at Oberhausen, but its flagship vineyard lies in the neighbouring village of Niederhausen.
The Nahe is a wine region of its own, not a part of the Mosel or of Rheinhessen.

wine.name: Monzinger Halenberg Riesling GG
wine.classification: VDP.Grosses Gewächs from the Halenberg, a VDP.Grosse Lage of Monzingen
wine.sites: The Halenberg east of Monzingen, a steep slope facing south to south west at about 160 to 220 metres, on weathered blue grey slate and quartzite that warms quickly in the sun.
wine.making: Picked by hand in selective passes and fermented dry, for the VDP requires every Grosses Gewächs to be dry by the legal measure; under the association's rule the wine may not be released before September of the year after the harvest.
wine.glass: Lime, white peach and green apple over smoky slate and crushed stone, with the blackcurrant leaf tang of the Nahe; taut and very dry, with a firm line of acidity and a long, saline finish.
wine.ageing: Tight and smoky when young, it needs five years or more to open and keeps for twenty years and beyond in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 10 to 13 degrees Celsius; no need to decant, though a young bottle gains from air in the glass; a large white wine glass.

label.means: The Halenberg vineyard of the village of Monzingen, the village name turned into an adjective.
Often shortened to GG: a dry wine of the VDP from a vineyard it ranks Grosse Lage.
Dry: the VDP requires every Grosses Gewächs to be dry by the legal measure.

records.table: Emrich-Schönleber's Monzinger Halenberg Riesling GG comes from a steep slope of blue slate and quartzite at Monzingen in the cooler upper Nahe. It is taut, smoky and lime scented, a dry wine that rewards five years in the cellar.
records.story: Monzingen lies in the upper Nahe, upstream of the famous middle valley, where the air is cooler and the grapes ripen later. The family behind the estate has grown vines here since the middle of the eighteenth century, by the accounts of the wine guide wein.plus and others, but for most of that time the vines were one crop among several. Between 1965 and 1985, father and son turned the farm into a pure wine estate, and the house gathered parcels in the Halenberg, a steep slope of blue slate and quartzite east of the village. By its own account it recovered much of that slope from decades of scrub, replanted it and made the name known again. The estate was admitted to the VDP in 1994, and the association ranks the Halenberg and the Frühlingsplätzchen among its Grosse Lage sites. Since the 2006 vintage the VDP has required its Grosses Gewächs to be dry by the legal measure, and the Halenberg is the house's dry wine to know: smoky slate, lime and nerve, the cool upper valley in a glass. For a sommelier it is the counterweight to the warmer middle Nahe, and the wine that shows how far upstream the region's quality runs.

others.name: Monzinger Frühlingsplätzchen Riesling GG
others.note: The rounder, more openly fruited of the house's two Grosse Lage wines.

others.name: Monzinger Halenberg Riesling Auslese

wine.name: Bockenauer Felseneck Riesling GG
wine.classification: VDP.Grosses Gewächs from the Felseneck, a VDP.Grosse Lage of Bockenau
wine.sites: The Felseneck above Bockenau, in the Ellerbach valley off the Nahe: a steep slope facing due south at about 250 to 310 metres, on blue Devonian slate with quartzite and basalt scree; the estate's sole property, by its own account.
wine.making: Picked by hand. By the house's own account its large Rieslings ferment only spontaneously, with the yeasts of the vineyard and the cellar, which gives the struck match reduction of their youth; under the VDP's rule the dry wine is released from September of the year after the harvest.
wine.glass: Struck match and flint at first, then white peach, lime and green apple over cold slate; dry, intense and taut, with piercing acidity and a long, stony finish.
wine.ageing: Reductive and closed when young, it opens after some years in bottle and keeps for twenty years and more in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 10 to 13 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour so the struck match reduction can lift; a white wine glass.

label.means: The Felseneck vineyard of the village of Bockenau, which lies off the Nahe in a side valley.
Often shortened to GG: a dry wine of the VDP from a vineyard it ranks Grosse Lage.
Dry: the VDP requires every Grosses Gewächs to be dry by the legal measure.

records.table: Schäfer-Fröhlich's Bockenauer Felseneck Riesling GG grows on a steep blue slate slope in a side valley of the Nahe and ferments with wild yeasts. Young, it smells of struck match and flint before the peach and lime come through, so give it air.
records.story: Bockenau lies off the Nahe itself, in the valley of the Ellerbach, and the Felseneck rises steeply above the village, facing due south. The family of the estate has grown vines here for more than two centuries, by its own account; the sources place its first records in the late eighteenth century without agreeing on a year. In 1995 a new generation took charge of the cellar, and the house made its name with Riesling fermented only with the native yeasts of vineyard and cellar, wines that smell of struck match and flint when young. It was admitted to the VDP in 2001, and the association ranks the Felseneck a Grosse Lage; the estate holds it alone, together with the Stromberg, also at Bockenau. Since the 2006 vintage the VDP has required its Grosses Gewächs to be dry by the legal measure, and the Felseneck GG is the house's dry wine to know. For a sommelier it teaches one lesson above all: the smoky reduction of a young bottle is a deliberate style of the house, born of its fermentation, and not a fault or a mark of the Nahe as a whole.

records.place: Niederhausen; the Kupfergrube at Schlossböckelheim, Nahe

wine.name: Schlossböckelheimer Kupfergrube Riesling GG
wine.classification: VDP.Grosses Gewächs from the Kupfergrube, a VDP.Grosse Lage of Schlossböckelheim
wine.sites: The Kupfergrube at Schlossböckelheim, a steep south facing slope on the site of a copper mine worked until 1901, its terraces cut into melaphyre, a dark volcanic rock that holds the heat, under a thin, stony soil.
wine.making: Picked by hand, crushed and pressed, then fermented spontaneously and matured partly in wood and partly in stainless steel. Since a vintage of the middle 2010s the house has held the Kupfergrube back in its deep cellar, releasing it at about five years old as a GG Reserve.
wine.glass: Lime, white peach and yellow apple over smoke and warm stone, with a dark, savoury edge from the volcanic rock; dry, firm and concentrated, with fresh, chiselled acidity and a long finish.
wine.ageing: Released only at about five years old, it seems youthful even then, as the house describes it, and keeps for two decades and more.
wine.serve: 10 to 13 degrees Celsius; no need to decant a bottle released with five years behind it; a white wine glass.

label.means: Copper mine: the vineyard was a working mine until 1901, before the Prussian domain planted it.
The village whose name the site carries, though the estate's cellar lies at Niederhausen.
Often shortened to GG: a dry wine of the VDP from a vineyard it ranks Grosse Lage.

records.table: Gut Hermannsberg's Schlossböckelheimer Kupfergrube Riesling GG grows on terraces cut into volcanic rock where a copper mine was worked until 1901. The house holds it back for about five years, so it reaches the table dry, firm and smoky, ready to open.
records.story: Copper was dug from the hillside at Schlossböckelheim until 1901, and the vineyard took the mine's name, Kupfergrube. In 1902 the Prussian state founded its royal wine domain on the Nahe at Niederhausen, the Königlich Preussische Weinbaudomäne, and set about turning the rocky ground into vineyards. Some 300,000 cubic metres of earth were moved and terraces cut into the rock, by the house's account with the labour of convicts, and the first harvest came some years later. The domain planted Riesling on the old mine and on the neighbouring slopes. After the Second World War it passed to the new state of Rhineland-Palatinate and was run as a state domain until it was privatised in 1998. New owners bought it in 2009 and named it Gut Hermannsberg, after the Hermannsberg, a vineyard at Niederhausen that is its sole property. In the middle of the 2010s the house began to hold the Kupfergrube Grosses Gewächs back in its deep cellar, releasing it at about five years old, since it holds that the wine shows its full range only with age. For a sommelier it is the history of German state domains told by one hill, and a lesson in volcanic Riesling.

The passing to Rhineland-Palatinate in 1946, the privatisation of 1998 and the sale of 2009 rest on wein.plus and Wines of Germany; the owners of 1998 and of 2009 are not named.

The holding back of the Kupfergrube to about five years is the house's own press: one summary dates the first such release to the 2017 vintage, a press headline to the 2016, so the record says a vintage of the middle 2010s. The plan asked whether the house still holds it back; the record tells it as a habit begun then, not as this year's rule of release.
Melaphyre as the bedrock is the house's own lexicon and site page; the VDP calls the Felsenberg's volcanic rock rhyolite, so the record does not name the rock for the Felsenberg.
The plan's wine name holds; the house prints it Kupfergrube Schlossböckelheim Riesling GG, site before village.

wine.name: Dorsheimer Goldloch Riesling GG
wine.classification: VDP.Grosses Gewächs from the Goldloch, a VDP.Grosse Lage of Dorsheim
wine.sites: The Goldloch at Dorsheim, a steep terraced slope facing south to south south west at about 140 to 210 metres, with many pebbles in a thin layer of loam over a stony conglomerate of the Permian Rotliegend.
wine.making: Picked by hand and fermented with native yeasts, then given a long rest in old Stückfass casks of oak from local forests, as the house describes it; under the VDP's rule the dry wine is released from September of the year after the harvest.
wine.glass: Ripe yellow apple, pear and lemon peel over a hint of flint and smoke; juicy and dry, with fresh acidity and a long, stony finish.
wine.ageing: Approachable within a few years, it keeps for twenty years and more; the house gives five to twenty five years after the harvest.
wine.serve: 10 to 13 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass.

label.means: The village and the site as the house prints them; older labels read Dorsheimer Goldloch.
Often shortened to GG: a dry wine of the VDP from a vineyard it ranks Grosse Lage.
Dry: the VDP requires every Grosses Gewächs to be dry by the legal measure.

records.table: Schlossgut Diel's Dorsheimer Goldloch Riesling GG comes from pebbly terraces at Dorsheim in the lower Nahe, fermented with native yeasts in old oak casks. It is juicy and yellow fruited, with a touch of flint, and it keeps for two decades.
records.story: Burg Layen is the ruin of a medieval castle above the lower Nahe, and the estate takes its name from it. In 1802, by the family's own account, a forebear of the Diels bought the castle and its land, and the family has held it since. For generations the estate was a mixed farm, and the vines grew slowly into its heart until wine became its whole business. Its fame rests on three vineyards at the neighbouring village of Dorsheim: the Goldloch, the Pittermännchen and the Burgberg, all ranked Grosse Lage by the VDP, which admitted the estate in 1989. The Goldloch differs from the Pittermännchen beside it, lying on pebbly loam over Permian conglomerate rather than slate, and gives a juicy Riesling with a touch of flint. The house also makes Sekt by the traditional method, and in February 2023 the association of traditional Sekt makers, the Verband traditioneller Sektmacher, admitted it as a member. Its Goldloch Riesling Sekt, from the same site, rests for years on its lees and is given no dosage. For a sommelier the Goldloch GG is the lower Nahe's answer to the slate of the middle valley, and a reminder that the region's soils change within a few kilometres.

others.name: Dorsheimer Burgberg Riesling GG

traps: Burg Layen is the estate's home, a castle and hamlet, not one of its vineyards; its three Grosse Lage sites lie at Dorsheim.
The Goldloch is pebbly loam over Permian conglomerate, not slate; the Pittermännchen beside it is weathered Devonian slate.

report: Not in the library. The purchase of 1802 is the house's own history (it gives 11 September) and Skurnik's; the seller, given as the Barons of Dalberg, rests on one clear source and is left out, as are the castle's own dates, which the sources give as twelfth or thirteenth century.

The doubt in the plan's note stands: one guide calls the Pittermännchen GG the house's flagship, and no source found ranks the Goldloch above it; the Goldloch is kept as the plan picked it, as one of three GGs the house presents as equals, with the Pittermännchen first among the others. A checker may propose the swap.

The Goldloch's soil is the VDP's (pebbles in thin loam over Rotliegend conglomerate); the house calls it very gravelly Permian primary rock, and one merchant says quartzite and slate, which is not kept.
The making is the house's own page for the 2024 GG; the Burgberg sheet of 2017 gives a single large cask of local oak and a year on fine lees in steel, which is not carried over to the Goldloch.
VDP admission in 1989 and the Sekt makers' admission of February 2023 are the house's own pages; the Sekt's 77 months on lees is one vintage's figure and is told only as years.
The members of the family, past heads included, are living or undated and are not named.

changed: wine.sites: the Goldloch faced south south west; now south to south south west, as the VDP and wein.plus give it.
story: the Goldloch was set against the other two Grosse Lage sites as not slate; now against the Pittermännchen beside it, since the Burgberg's soil was not read.
open: The buyer of 1802 is named Johann Peter Diel (1750 to 1811) by wein.plus alone; the story keeps a forebear of the Diels.
The Goldloch stays the pick over the Pittermännchen, which one guide calls the house's leading dry wine; the house presents its three GGs as equals.
